claims.text: Consciousness corresponds to a system's capacity to integrate information: it requires a large repertoire of possible states that cannot be decomposed into causally independent subsystems.
evidence_excerpts: If consciousness corresponds to the capacity to integrate information, then a physical system should be able to generate consciousness to the extent that it has a large repertoire of available states (information), yet it cannot be decomposed into a collection of causally independent subsystems (integration).

claims.text: The quantity of consciousness available to a system is measured by the Φ value of a complex, defined as the effective information integrated across the subset's minimum information bipartition.
evidence_excerpts: The information integration for subset S, or Φ(S), is simply the (non-normalized) value of EI(A G B) for the minimum information bipartition: Φ(S) = EI(MIBA G B).
Specifically, a complex is a subset S having Φ>0 that is not included within a larger subset having higher Φ.

claims.text: A conscious entity is identified with a complex: a subset of elements with Φ greater than zero that is not contained within a larger subset of higher Φ, with the main complex being the highest-Φ complex in the system.
evidence_excerpts: What we are left with are complexes – individual entities that can integrate information. Specifically, a complex is a subset S having Φ>0 that is not included within a larger subset having higher Φ.
Of the complexes that make up a given system, the one with the maximum value of Φ(S) is called the main complex.

claims.text: The quality of a conscious experience is determined by the informational relationships among elements of the main complex, as captured by the effective information matrix rather than by Φ alone.
evidence_excerpts: Note that the effective information matrix is different for the two complexes, even though Φ is the same. The effective information matrix defines the set of informational relationships, or 'qualia space' for each complex.
Although the states are identical for the two complexes, their meaning is different because of the difference in the effective information matrix.

claims.text: A particular conscious experience is specified by the activity state of the variables that mediate effective informational relationships within the main complex at that time.
evidence_excerpts: The relevant activity variables are those that mediate the informational relationships among the elements, that is, those that mediate effective information. For example, if the elements are local groups of neurons, then the relevant variables are their firing patterns over tens to hundreds of milliseconds.
Different conscious states correspond to different patterns of activity distributed over all the elements of a complex, with no contribution from elements outside.

claims.text: Human consciousness is generated by a distributed thalamocortical network because that network combines functional specialization with functional integration.
evidence_excerpts: It would seem, therefore, that the neural substrate of consciousness is a distributed thalamocortical network, and that there is no single cortical area where it all comes together.

Connection matrices yielding the highest values of information integration (Φ = 74 bits) share two key characteristics. First, connection patterns are different for different elements, ensuring functional specialization. Second, all elements can be reached from all other elements of the network, ensuring functional integration.

claims.text: The cerebellum contributes little directly to conscious experience because its modular organization yields many small low-Φ complexes rather than one large high-Φ complex.
evidence_excerpts: This network yields Φ = 20 bits for each of its three modules, which form the system's three complexes. This example indicates that, irrespective of how many elements and connections are present in a neural structure, if that structure is organized in a strongly modular manner with little interactions among modules, complex size and Φ values are necessarily low.
According to the information integration theory, this is the reason why these systems, although computationally very sophisticated, contribute little to consciousness.

claims.text: During slow wave sleep, consciousness is reduced because neurophysiological changes lower neuronal readiness and make network responses less differentiated even when anatomical connectivity remains intact.
evidence_excerpts: During slow wave sleep, average firing rates of cortical neurons are also similar to those observed during quiet wakefulness. However, due to changes in the level of certain neuromodulators, virtually all cortical neurons engage in slow oscillations at around 1 Hz, which are reflected in slow waves in the EEG.

Even if the anatomical connectivity of a complex stays the same, a change in key parameters governing the readiness of neurons to respond and the differentiation of their responses may alter radically the Φ value of the complex, with corresponding consequences on consciousness.

claims.text: Conscious experience requires sufficient time for effective interactions to build across the main complex, with thalamocortical differentiated responses emerging over tens to hundreds of milliseconds.
evidence_excerpts: The theory predicts that the time requirements for the generation of conscious experience in the brain emerge directly from the time requirements for the build-up of effective interactions among the elements of the main complex.

In a model including nine functionally segregated visual areas, the time it takes for functionally specialized neurons located in several different areas to interact constructively and produce a specific, correlated firing pattern is at least 80 milliseconds.

claims.text: Consciousness is a graded property of physical systems and could in principle exist in natural or artificial systems to the extent that they contain a complex of high Φ.
evidence_excerpts: Any physical system has subjective experience to the extent that it is capable of integrating information, irrespective of what it is made of.
It follows that consciousness is not an all-or-none property, but it is graded: to varying degrees, it should exist in most natural (and artificial) systems.

evidence_items.title: Effective Information Equation
evidence_items.excerpt: Specifically, we define the effective information between A and B as EI(A→B) = MI(AHmax;B). Here MI(A;B) = H(A) + H(B) - H(AB) stands for mutual information, a measure of the entropy or information shared between a source (A) and a target (B).
evidence_items.overview: This formal definition supplies the mathematical bridge between causal perturbation and information. It matters because the theory does not treat consciousness as raw entropy; it asks how much differentiated causal influence one part of a system can have on another. The excerpt grounds the later definition of Φ in mutual information and makes clear that the measure concerns possible causal effects rather than only observed states.

evidence_items.title: Phi Minimum Bipartition
evidence_items.excerpt: The minimum information bipartition MIBA G B of subset S – its 'weakest link' – is its bipartition for which the normalized effective information reaches a minimum, corresponding to min{EI(A G B)/Hmax(A G B)}. The information integration for subset S, or Φ(S), is simply the (non-normalized) value of EI(A G B) for the minimum information bipartition: Φ(S) = EI(MIBA G B).
evidence_items.overview: This passage is the central formal artifact for the paper's quantity claim. It explains why Φ is assessed at the informational weakest link: a system only integrates information to the extent that information remains causally effective across its least integrated partition. The formula also limits the claim by tying Φ to a chosen subset and bipartition procedure, not to a direct behavioral or introspective readout.

evidence_items.title: Complex Selection Rule
evidence_items.excerpt: What we are left with are complexes – individual entities that can integrate information. Specifically, a complex is a subset S having Φ>0 that is not included within a larger subset having higher Φ. For a complex, and only for a complex, it is appropriate to say that, when it enters a particular state out of its repertoire, it generates an amount of integrated information corresponding to its Φ value. Of the complexes that make up a given system, the one with the maximum value of Φ(S) is called the main complex.
evidence_items.overview: The excerpt gives the theory's identity criterion for conscious entities. It prevents arbitrary assignment of consciousness to every active part of a system by excluding subsets contained in larger higher-Φ subsets. It also introduces the main complex, which the later neurobiological interpretation uses to distinguish direct contributors to experience from inputs, outputs, and modulators.

evidence_items.title: Qualia Space Matrix
evidence_items.excerpt: Shown are two systems, one with a 'divergent' architecture and one with a 'chain' architecture. The analysis of complexes shows that both contain a complex of four elements having a Φ value of 10. Note that the effective information matrix is different for the two complexes, even though Φ is the same. The effective information matrix defines the set of informational relationships, or 'qualia space' for each complex. Although the states are identical for the two complexes, their meaning is different because of the difference in the effective information matrix.
evidence_items.overview: This figure result separates quantity from quality. Two complexes can have equal Φ while differing in the organization of effective information, so the paper uses the matrix of internal informational relationships to account for the character or meaning of experience. The result is schematic, but it is independently meaningful because it shows why a scalar consciousness quantity alone cannot specify experiential content.

evidence_items.title: Thalamocortical Optimization Result
evidence_items.excerpt: Connection matrices yielding the highest values of information integration (Φ = 74 bits) share two key characteristics. First, connection patterns are different for different elements, ensuring functional specialization. Second, all elements can be reached from all other elements of the network, ensuring functional integration. If functional specialization is lost by replacing the heterogeneous connectivity with a homogeneous one, or if functional integration is lost by rearranging the connections to form small modules, the value of Φ decreases considerably.
evidence_items.overview: This simulation result supports the claim that high Φ depends jointly on specialization and integration. It also explains why thalamocortical anatomy is a plausible substrate: differentiated local functions are embedded in reciprocal interactions. The evidence is model-based rather than a direct measurement of a human brain, so its scope is to illustrate a mechanistic requirement rather than to prove the full neurobiological assignment.

evidence_items.title: Cerebellar Modularity Result
evidence_items.excerpt: A strongly modular network, consisting of three modules of eight strongly interconnected elements each, yields Φ = 20 bits for each of its three modules, which form the system's three complexes. This example indicates that, irrespective of how many elements and connections are present in a neural structure, if that structure is organized in a strongly modular manner with little interactions among modules, complex size and Φ values are necessarily low. Figure 4a also describes a cerebellum-like organization with three separate complexes with low values of Φ (Φ = 20 bits) and a large complex encompassing all the elements with extremely low Φ (Φ = 5 bits).
evidence_items.overview: This evidence links anatomical organization to the cerebellum puzzle. The cerebellum has many neurons and synapses, but the model result says modular, weakly interacting patches do not form a large high-Φ complex. The argument therefore predicts low direct contribution to consciousness despite computational sophistication; the limitation is that the figure is a simplified neural-like architecture, not a full cerebellar connectome measurement.

evidence_items.title: Slow Wave Sleep Bistability
evidence_items.excerpt: During slow wave sleep, average firing rates of cortical neurons are also similar to those observed during quiet wakefulness. However, due to changes in the level of certain neuromodulators, virtually all cortical neurons engage in slow oscillations at around 1 Hz, which are reflected in slow waves in the EEG. In the sleep mode, the network becomes bistable: specific effects of different perturbations are quickly washed out and their propagation impeded; the whole network transitions into the depolarized or into the hyperpolarized phase of the slow oscillation, a stereotypic response that is observed irrespective of the particular perturbation.
evidence_items.overview: The sleep evidence matters because it shows that activity level alone is not enough for consciousness. Tononi uses slow wave sleep to argue that the same network can lose conscious capacity when response readiness and differentiation collapse. The evidence supports a mechanistic account of reduced consciousness, while preserving the nuance that REM sleep and some slow-wave awakenings can still involve experience.

evidence_items.title: Conscious Timing Results
evidence_items.excerpt: Studies of how a percept is progressively specified and stabilized indicate that it takes up to 100–200 milliseconds to develop a fully formed sensory experience. Experiments in which the somatosensory areas of the cerebral cortex were stimulated directly indicate that low intensity stimuli must be sustained for up to 500 milliseconds to produce a conscious sensation. Multi-unit recordings in the primary visual cortex of monkeys show that after 80–100 milliseconds, their discharge accurately predicts the conscious detection of the figure. In a model including nine functionally segregated visual areas, the time it takes for functionally specialized neurons located in several different areas to interact constructively and produce a specific, correlated firing pattern is at least 80 milliseconds.
evidence_items.overview: This collection of timing results anchors the theory's temporal scale. Consciousness is predicted to require time for causal interactions to build, not merely instantaneous firing in isolated neurons. The excerpt combines psychophysics, direct stimulation, recordings, and simulation, so it is broad but heterogeneous evidence; it supports a tens-to-hundreds-of-milliseconds window rather than a single exact threshold.

relations.rationale: The Φ measure operationalizes the broader integrated-information account of consciousness.
The complex rule identifies the system subset to which the Φ quantity applies.
Φ addresses quantity, while the effective-information matrix addresses quality.
The thalamocortical case is the theory's principal neurobiological application.
The cerebellum is used as a counterexample showing that many neurons are insufficient without integration.
The activity state specifies experience only over a temporal scale sufficient for effective interactions.

summary: Giulio Tononi's 2004 BMC Neuroscience article formulates an information integration theory of consciousness. The source identifies consciousness with a system's capacity to integrate information, defines Φ through effective information across a minimum information bipartition, and uses the notion of complexes to specify which physical subset counts as the conscious entity. It distinguishes quantity of consciousness, measured by Φ, from quality, determined by the effective-information relationships among elements in a complex. The article applies the theory to thalamocortical organization, cerebellar modularity, sleep, seizures, timing constraints, and the possibility of graded consciousness in nonhuman or artificial systems.

source_dossier.summary_short: Tononi's article proposes that consciousness is identical with integrated information. It formalizes a measure, Φ, for the amount of integrated causal information generated by a complex, then uses that framework to explain why thalamocortical networks, but not similarly large modular systems such as the cerebellum, are central to conscious experience.
source_dossier.summary_long: This source is an early full statement of information integration theory. It begins from two phenomenological properties: conscious experience is highly differentiated because each experience rules out an enormous repertoire of alternatives, and it is integrated because each experience is given as a unified whole rather than as independent fragments. Tononi argues that a physical substrate of consciousness must therefore have many possible states while resisting decomposition into causally independent parts. The proposed measure, Φ, attempts to capture this conjunction by asking how much effective information remains across a subset's minimum information bipartition, its informational weakest link. A subset with Φ greater than zero that is not contained in a larger higher-Φ subset is a complex; the highest-Φ complex is the main complex and is treated as the direct substrate of consciousness. The paper then separates the amount of consciousness from its content. Φ measures quantity, while the pattern of effective information among the elements of the complex forms a structured 'qualia space' that determines experiential quality; the activity state of the relevant variables within that structure specifies the particular experience at a given time. The neurobiological argument uses the thalamocortical system as the central example because it combines functional specialization with reciprocal integration across distributed areas. By contrast, the cerebellum, despite its enormous number of neurons and computational sophistication, is described as modular and therefore unlikely to form a large high-Φ complex. The same logic is applied to reticular arousal systems, sensory afferents, motor outputs, and cortico-subcortical loops: they can influence consciousness without directly belonging to the main complex. The discussion of sleep and timing emphasizes that anatomy is not enough. Slow wave sleep can reduce consciousness because response readiness and differentiation collapse, and conscious percepts require tens to hundreds of milliseconds for effective interactions to build. The article closes with broad implications: consciousness is graded, potentially present in infants, animals, and artificial systems, and measurable in principle where verbal report is unavailable, though practical measurement remains difficult.

sections.heading: Core Argument
sections.body: The article's core proposition is that consciousness is not merely information, activity, reportability, or behavioral output. It is the capacity of a physical system to integrate information so that many possible states are available to the system as a whole and cannot be reduced to independent component repertoires. This is why Tononi contrasts a camera sensor with a brain: both may discriminate many inputs, but only the brain-like system has internal causal dependence sufficient for integration.

sections.heading: Formal Measure
sections.body: The formal machinery defines effective information by perturbing one part of a system and measuring the differentiated effects on another part. Φ is then assigned to a subset by finding the minimum information bipartition and taking the effective information across that weakest link. This makes the proposed quantity sensitive to both specialization and integration; a system fails if it has many states but no causal unity, or unity without differentiated causal structure.

sections.heading: Conscious Entity Boundary
sections.body: Tononi's concept of a complex provides a boundary rule for conscious subjects. A subset counts as a complex only if it has Φ greater than zero and is not nested inside a larger subset with higher Φ. This rule is used to distinguish direct constituents of experience from ports, modulators, afferents, and efferents that can affect the main complex without themselves contributing dimensions to experience.

sections.heading: Quality and Content
sections.body: The paper does not reduce conscious quality to a single scalar. Two systems can have the same Φ yet different effective-information matrices, and therefore different qualia spaces. The particular conscious state is specified by the activity variables that mediate informational interactions inside that structured space. This lets the theory explain why the same activation pattern can have different meaning depending on the surrounding causal organization.

sections.heading: Neurobiological Fit
sections.body: The thalamocortical system is treated as the best biological candidate because it combines differentiated local specializations with dense reciprocal interactions across areas. Tononi uses simulations to show that high Φ requires heterogeneous connectivity and reachability among elements. The cerebellum provides the complementary case: high neuron count and computational sophistication do not suffice if organization remains modular and interactions across modules are weak.

sections.heading: State Dependence
sections.body: The source emphasizes that anatomical connectivity is only one condition. During slow wave sleep, cortical neurons can have average firing rates similar to quiet wakefulness, yet slow oscillations and bistable responses reduce differentiated causal effects. This supports the claim that the same thalamocortical network can generate much or little consciousness depending on readiness, differentiation, and functional connectivity.

sections.heading: Temporal Constraint
sections.body: The theory imposes a temporal scale on consciousness. Effective interactions across the main complex need time to build, so instantaneous or very brief activity is not enough. The paper aligns this with microgenesis, cortical stimulation, monkey visual recordings, and thalamocortical simulations, all pointing to tens or hundreds of milliseconds as the relevant window for differentiated integrated responses.

sections.heading: Implications and Limits
sections.body: Tononi treats consciousness as graded and potentially substrate-independent: any physical system could have experience to the extent that it supports a high-Φ complex. The source also acknowledges major practical limits, especially measuring Φ in real brains and developing the biological details needed for memory, language, selfhood, and higher-order aspects of consciousness. The article is therefore both a formal proposal and a research program.
